articles.title: Trump invites Haley Stevens to join GOP as Democrats condemn her 'betrayal'
articles.summary: Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate from Michigan, and Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens speak to reporters outside Perfecting Church in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. —Emily Elconin—Bloomberg/Getty Images President Donald Trump invited outgoing congresswoman Haley Stevens, a longtime Michigan Democrat, to join the Republican Party after she surprisingly endorsed her state’s GOP nominee for the U.S. Senate, Mike Rogers, in a last-minute move her partymates have called a “betrayal.” “I don’t know Haley, I’ve never met Haley,” Trump said at a rally in Iowa on Sunday, the final weekend before the Nov. 3 midterm elections . “But Haley said what few people are willing to say. I think I’d probably—I’d love her to join the Republican Party actually.” Stevens ran for the U.S. Senate seat herself but lost the Democratic primary to progressive Abdul El-Sayed in August. While she initially congratulated and offered her support to El-Sayed for the general election, the two have been at odds, primarily over concerns about antisemitism, which Stevens has accused El-Sayed, who is Muslim , of not denouncing strongly enough. On Friday, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce a controversial ad that blamed Michigan’s cost-of-living issues on U.S. aid to Israel. El-Sayed, whose campaign was not behind the ad though it supported his candidacy, responded with a statement that the focus of his campaign is on the “challenges Michiganders are facing” and defeating Rogers, while Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” He told reporters that he did not agree with the ad’s contents but did not want to “play the condemn game” about an unaffiliated ad. Stevens was supposed to appear with El-Sayed at a planned Democratic campaign event on Sunday, but Rep. Debbie Dingell (D, Mich.) said in an interview that before the event, she disinvited Stevens on account of her strained relationship with El-Sayed. “There’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place,” Dingell said Saturday. On Sunday, Stevens appeared instead at an event at Perfecting Church in Detroit with Rogers. “Our Democratic nominee for Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video posted on social media later that morning. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” On CNN on Sunday night, Stevens attempted to explain her move, saying it was because of El-Sayed’s “anger and lack of kindness.” She cited his past associations with controversial political influencer Hasan Piker and Piker’s uncle Cenk Uygur, whose Rebellion PAC was behind the recent anti-Israel ad. She insisted that she is “trying to help” the Democratic Party by turning on El-Sayed, whom she compared to Graham Platner , the former scandal-plagued Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from Maine who withdrew from that race in July. Stevens said she remains a “really proud Democrat” who “absolutely” wants Democrats to win control of the Senate, but her shock announcement of an endorsement for the GOP candidate just days before Election Day could upend a tight race that may decide the fate of the upper chamber. Democrats denounce, Republicans pounce Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer slammed what he called Stevens’ “despicable betrayal,” posting on social media that Senate Democrats were “united” in their support for El-Sayed. Other Democrats have also shared their dismay and disappointment. House Speaker Emerita and veteran California Democrat Rep. Nancy Pelosi said on social media that Stevens “has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.” Elissa Slotkin, Michigan’s Democratic Senator elected in 2024 and a former House colleague of Stevens from the same 2018 blue wave that saw a record number of women elected to Congress, posted on social media : “Anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good.” Ex-Rep. Susan Wild (D, Pa.), also elected in 2018 and formerly a roommate with Stevens in Washington, said in an emotional post about the Rogers endorsement that “the fallout for Haley won’t just be in Dem politics; she will be a pariah among her friends in the Democratic caucus in Congress.” Ex-Rep. Andy Levin, a Michigan Democrat who was elected alongside Stevens in 2018 but after redistricting lost to her in a 2022 primary, posted that Haley’s endorsement of Rogers was “unconscionable, beyond the pale.” Stevens’ chief of staff and multiple other staffers resigned on Sunday. “I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate,” Justin German, Stevens’ former chief of staff of eight years wrote in a statement . “This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines.” Stevens’ communications director Logan Basch, appears to have also left his post: his email sent back an auto-reply to TIME that read, “Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens.” The Michigan Democratic Party also appeared to have distanced from Stevens, with state party chair Curtis Hertel posting on social media Sunday: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” Republicans immediately jumped on the opportunity, which could offer a late boost amid an election year where retaining the majority in either chamber of Congress has looked unlikely . Rogers touted Stevens’ endorsement on social media , adding that she “showed courage and bravery in putting Michigan first” and that he’s “grateful for her support.” House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Sunday as he flanked Trump upon his arrival in Iowa that he sent Stevens a note commending “how courageous she was, how much we appreciate that she’s standing for truth.” For his part, El-Sayed, who leads Rogers in public opinion polling , has appeared unfazed by Stevens’ actions, telling reporters : “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.” —Rebecca Schneid contributed reporting. This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/11/02/haley-stevens-abdul-el-sayed-mike-rogers-endorsement-trump-republicans-democrats/

articles.title: 4 Americans among dozens killed in last week's train crash in Spain, officials say
articles.summary: Four United States citizens were among the at least 69 people who were killed when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain last week, officials said Sunday. The Center for Integrated Data, the legal body in Spain in charge of identifying victims of events with a high death toll, said on Sunday night that the casualties in the country's second deadly rail collision this year also included one citizen each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Two citizens of Australia and a citizen of Japan remain missing, the Agence France-Presse and local media reported. The center, which had already announced the deaths of a French and Portuguese citizen as well as 54 Spaniards, said that all but three of the victims had been identified. "As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country," the statement said, AFP reported. The crash occurred on the morning of Oct. 28 in Urda, in the province of Toledo, when the high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars. Officials said 58 people were injured. The two trains, with more than 540 people on board, were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville. Transport Minister Óscar Puente has blamed a traffic controller's poor judgment for much of what went wrong. However, railway unions have pushed back, citing deteriorating working conditions. They say too few controllers are handling growing workloads, making it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of millions of passengers. The independent investigators said their initial findings indicated that the state-owned RENFE train was moving at between 100 and 125 mph when it struck the privately owned IRYO train. It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January , more than two hours farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation. Spain's high-speed rail network, the world's second-largest after China's, has long been regarded as a success of state industrial policy. Until this year, it had recorded no fatal crashes since entering service more than three decades ago. articles.title: Trump to deliver final midterm pitch at problem-plagued Lincoln Memorial pool
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day . In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.” “We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he'd be giving a speech there Monday afternoon. Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious. The unusual move marks a departure from Trump's month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war , high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats . Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was “my last stop.” The presidewnt spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation's capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes , demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom , converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad. Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building , has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course . He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he's spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time. Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day. The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump's early estimate — and that's assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future. Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms , and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July. Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship . In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool “was vandalized badly.” He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that. Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible. A judge later permanently dismissed it. That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro “choked,” and that he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella” — though he stopped short of firing her. articles.title: All 9 people on board plane killed after it crashes in Florida, federal officials say
articles.summary: A Learjet that Gov. Ron DeSantis said looked "like a missile going down" crashed Sunday near Greenacres killing all nine aboard and leaving a large swath of the area in fire and scattered debris. The plane, according to federal authorities, had departed Austin, Texas and was headed to the Bahamas. The plane crashed into a mobile home neighborhood around 12:50 p.m. in the area of Military Trail and 10th Avenue North, causing debris across a large area, but, according to DeSantis, no reported injuries or deaths from people on the ground. DeSantis was at the crash site Sunday evening and described it as a "cataclysmic plane crash." More: 'We're gonna crash! ... 'We're out of time' among last words from pilot More: Thunderstorms were firing on Sunday near where a Lear jet went down More: Learjet jet crash that killed nine was 'cataclysmic,' DeSantis says The governor said federal aviation officials were expected in Palm Beach County as soon as Sunday night and would conduct their investigation into the cause. All nine people aboard the plane died, said Sean Duffy, the U.S. secretary of transportation, in a post on X, formerly Twitter, just before 4 p.m. He called the crash a "horrific tragedy." The FAA said the Learjet 60 departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. “We’re out of time,” the pilot can be heard saying in air traffic control audio circulated online shortly before the Learjet crashed near Greenacres. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate. The NTSB will be in charge of the investigation and will provide all updates. The incident closed all lanes of Military Trail in the area of Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said. FL | PALM BEACH COUNTY First VIDEO of unknown type plane crash in Greenacre. @EmergencyStream pic.twitter.com/M2fsW45I9h — EmergencyStream (@EmergencyStream) November 1, 2026 Authorities said motorists should are avoid the area and seek alternate routes. Postings on Facebook show a fairly wide swath of area spotted with fires, debris and what looks like a crater in the ground. A video circulating online of a plane making a nosedive into the ground is said to be the Learjet, but The Palm Beach Post is not sharing that video as it has not been confirmed. The video is said to be from a driver's dashcam video. The cause of the crash is unknown. Some chatter on social media raised the suspicion that the plane could have been shot down because flight restrictions were in place as President Donald Trump was in town this weekend . Trump departed President Donald J. Trump International Airport for Iowa around noon. More Aftermath of Palm Beach County plane crash. @EmergencyStream pic.twitter.com/kxN1AzltLa — EmergencyStream (@EmergencyStream) November 1, 2026 The Palm Beach Post reported recently that military air defense systems have been positioned around the president's Mar-a-Lago club and home and the surrounding area. Planes that fly into the restricted airspace are diverted, usually by military jets. Multiple planes have violated the airspace since Trump first took office, but a plane has never been shot down in Palm Beach County because of the airspace violations. The upgraded security systems, a pair of Avenger Air Defense Systems , are positioned on a floating barge in the Lake Worth Lagoon on the west side of Trump's Mar-a-Lago. A separate bank of Avenger Air Defense Systems are positioned on the south side of Trump international airport, near the area where Air Force One parks during Trump's visits to Palm Beach. Aircraft Incident. Military Trail between Cresthaven and 10th Avenue N closed to all traffic. Avoid the area. This will be an extended incident. pic.twitter.com/lhl6yY1A0U — PBC Fire Rescue (@PBCFR) November 1, 2026 Each Avenger comprises a modified Humvee equipped with a rotating turret that has two pods capable of launching short-range infrared-homing Stinger missiles, according to a U.S. Army website. The Avenger's targets could include cruise missiles, drones, helicopters and low-flying and high-speed fixed-wing aircraft, according to the Army. As of Sunday night, there was no indication the Learjet was shot down. Weather conditions in the West Palm Beach area on Sunday afternoon were rough with thunderstorms widespread because a stalled frontal boundary parked over the area, pushing freezing cloud tops tens of thousands of feet high — a situation that can cause icing trouble with equipment but also from severe turbulence. The crash site is in an unincorporated area near Greenacres and Palm Springs. The Village of Palm Springs said it has officials on the scene monitoring any effect the crash will have on water and sewer services. If residents experience disruptions, they should call the Utilities Department at (561) 584-8200. Check back for updates on this Breaking News story. articles.title: A record number of doctors and nurses are running for office. What's driving them?
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, Amy Acton, Xavier Becerra and Kristin Hook are among the candidates with healthcare backgrounds in this year's midterm elections. - Getty Images/Reuters/AP At least 125 doctors, nurses and public health experts are on the ballot for Tuesday’s midterm elections — an unprecedented number from fields that historically offered fewer paths to elected office than boardrooms and courtrooms. Their campaigns emerged in the aftermath of Covid-19, when doctors and health officials were celebrated at first, overwhelmed by work and tragedy for years, and in some cases, targeted because of distrust or politics around their messages. Some candidates say they realized during that time how their training and expertise in health and science were more closely tied to government and politics than they’d thought. “One of the things you learn to do in medicine is to listen and sit with somebody in pain and help them to clarify what the opportunities are, based on your knowledge about how the body or their health works, and I find that the work of politics is really quite similar,” said Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former health director for Wayne County, Michigan, who is running for US Senate against Republican Mike Rogers. Democrat US Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed says medicine and politics both involve listening and helping people. - Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images Dr. Amy Acton, a preventive medicine specialist who served as Republican Gov. Mike DeWine’s high-profile public health director in Ohio, is running for governor as a Democrat against biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican. Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former congressman who served as President Joe Biden’s secretary of health and human services, is vying for the governor in California against Republican media personality Steve Hilton. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and pediatrician in South Carolina, is running for US Senate against Republican Sen. Darline Graham. There are candidates with industry experience too, including healthcare attorney Cinde Warmington, a Democrat running to be New Hampshire’s governor, and Republican Rick Jackson, founder and CEO of Jackson Healthcare, who’s running to be Georgia’s governor. “I haven’t seen anything exactly like this before,” said historian Dr. Kristoffer Shields , director of the Eagleton Center on the American Governor at Rutgers University. “The link between science and politics has always been sort of weak.” Less than 10% of the current Congress has a medical, public health or engineering degree. By comparison, 47% of senators and 31% of House members have law degrees. Congress does have tiny but active Republican and Democratic doctors’ caucuses. Four people with health backgrounds — all Republicans and doctors — serve in the US Senate: Wyoming’s John Barrasso, Louisiana’s Bill Cassidy, Kansas’ Roger Marshall and Kentucky’s Rand Paul. The House has 17 physicians, four dentists, two pharmacists , a nurse practitioner , an optometrist and a rehabilitation therapist. At the state level, the ranks are even thinner, and they’ve been shrinking. Only about 3% of state legislators had medical, science or engineering backgrounds as of March 2025, according to a Rutgers analysis of the Scientists in State Politics Database. That’s down 25% from the year before. Hawaii’s Josh Green is the sole US governor with a medical degree, and no governors have a public health degree. No doctor has ever been president; the ninth president, William Henry Harrison, went to medical school but dropped out when he ran out of money to pay for it, and became a soldier instead. Unprecedented interest Something seemed to change this year, said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, a political action committee that recruits, trains and helps Democrats with science, tech, engineering and math backgrounds get elected. His group has been flooded with support requests. “We’ve had over 700 applications from people who want to run for office. To put that in context, it’s usually been like 200 every election cycle,” Polyak said. The American Medical Association has long encouraged people in the profession to get involved in politics. It has two political education programs: a candidate workshop and a campaign school for members. Cassidy and Barrasso are graduates, as are US Reps. Ami Bera and Mariannette Miller-Meeks. “Advocacy is strongest when physicians themselves are in the room where decisions are made. As is often noted, ‘If you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,’” AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in an email to CNN. “More physicians running for office is a good sign. We don’t think of ourselves as politicians, but we advocate for our patients every day because of prior authorization or other obstacles that prevent them from receiving care. We are accustomed to relentless advocacy.” Public health saw a similar surge in candidate interest. “I started getting calls in January and February a year ago, asking me for advice,” said Dr. Kristin Hook, a former staffer at the US National Institutes of Health and the US Government Accountability Office. She lost the first time she ran as a Democrat for Texas’ 21st Congressional District, in 2024, but is on the ballot again this year for the same seat. Democratic congressional candidate Dr. Kristin Hook says other would-be hopefuls have asked her advice, based on her experience running in 2024. - Joel Angel Juarez/Reuters “People from all across the country wanted to run, and they wanted to know what I did and what I learned,” she said. “I had these little chats with a bunch of public health folks, all different, and many former feds who wanted to prevent what we’re seeing right now.” One strong motivator for Hook to run for office was what she sees as an attack on science by the Trump administration. “Our country should be great. Our country should be pro-science, pro-innovation, and science keeps us safe. It protects us. It leads to wonderful discoveries, and this administration has completely burned all of that down,” she said. Hook points to the firing of thousands of federal doctors and scientists, cuts to billions in research funding, the removal of entire government datasets and public health websites, and the undermining of longstanding public health measures like water fluoridation and childhood vaccines . Along with gas prices, healthcare is the biggest household expense worrying voters, polls show . Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” is expected to cut insurance to 10 million more people , one of the biggest rollbacks in health insurance coverage ever, experts say . Many of the candidates with healthcare backgrounds, like most Americans surveyed, say they disapprove of the current leadership at HHS. California gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, HHS secretary under President Joe Biden, says the agency is "not a place for science deniers." - Grace Widyatmadja/CNN “HHS is not a place for science deniers or science skeptics,” Becerra told CNN earlier this year. “Why would you get rid of some of our best scientists and doctors and health professionals? “I think it’s a prescription for a real disaster,” he added. “We deal with enough natural disasters, having to help with hurricanes, having to address pandemics, that’s bad enough. But when you put on top of that these man-made disasters, then you know that America’s health and America’s economy are at risk.” Pandemic politics The pandemic was also a major driver for many of the healthcare professionals now seeking office. “They’ve been under heavy political fire and either survived it or have moved on and learned from it, and it’s made them that much stronger,” said Lori Tremmel Freeman, CEO of the National Association of County and City Health Officials. Typically, public health leaders play a vital role that’s out of the spotlight. But the pandemic pushed many onto everyone’s television. For some, the attention brought death threats and hate mail, and a record number quit . Others emerged as local folk heroes. Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, touts her work alongside Republican Gov. Mike DeWine during the Covid-19 pandemic. - Jeff Swensen/Getty Images Acton says she faced a handful of protesters at her home but mostly felt support from Ohioans, many of whom watched her daily briefings with DeWine, the Republican governor. During the pandemic, her image appeared on T-shirts and a mural, and a bobblehead ad quoted the Dayton Daily News describing her as “Ohio’s trusted face during the pandemic.” A 2020 New York Times editorial called Acton “the leader we wish we all had.” “The love in this state was so much greater than any of the hate,” she said. “It was an honor to work alongside Gov. Mike DeWine. We were totally focused on saving lives, and we definitely put people’s health and well-being over politics.” But it may be hard for public health leaders and doctors to win over voters aggrieved by pandemic-era vaccine policies, masking rules and shuttered schools and businesses. “Especially on the Republican side, I think there’s a lot more distrust of the medical profession post-Covid,” said Woodrow Johnston, a political consultant for Republican politicians. “A lot of Republicans feel they were misled or even lied to when it came to government shutdowns.” Polls show that Democrats have more confidence in scientists than Republicans. However, one Pew poll found that trust dipped during the pandemic and has ticked up more recently. Another 2026 Pew survey found that scientists are more trusted to act in the public interest than journalists, business leaders and elected officials. Not everyone realizes how much political skill public health leaders must wield to win support for their solutions, Freeman says. The pandemic tested many of them. “We serve everyone everywhere in every single community, no matter what their political leaning,” she said. “To have somebody with all of this wealth of experience in different areas would help all across the board, and not just health programs. Even just to help people understand that healthiness really drives economic prosperity.” Johnston said he has helped more Republican candidates with medical or public health backgrounds win office lately. Such candidates can connect with certain voters. “Sometimes, smart people like smart people,” Johnston said. And their scientific expertise is needed, said Shields, the historian. Some problems are straightforward health issues, such as lack of access to care. Other problems are more existential: how to govern AI so it’s safe, how to find renewable energy and how to address the climate crisis. “There’s so many issues that we’re facing where we need people with scientific expertise in the room,” he said. Acton says that having health professionals in higher office can help people’s health, perhaps even more than an individual doctor can help a patient. She thinks of the average lifespan in the US: Advances in medicine and technology account for some improvements, but a lot of it’s also due to “things that we had to solve together.” “It was things like clean water, safe food, child labor laws, public school for every kid, traffic safety laws – the list goes on and on,” Acton said. “That’s what government’s role is: a big catalyzer and convener.” She said it was clear to her while working with DeWine during Covid-19 that the governor’s job was about protecting the health and well-being of everyone. “Just like being a doctor, we’re for all patients. Being governor is actually about improving those social and economic and environmental determinants of our well-being and our prosperity,” Acton said. “It’s funny. You think of it as so different, but I really realized it’s actually exactly what I’ve been trained to do.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/01/health/health-candidates-midterms

articles.title: Severe weather could complicate voting in several key states on Tuesday
articles.summary: Millions of Americans will head to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and the weather will be working in their favor across much of the country. However, rain and thunderstorms could complicate travel plans in parts of the southern United States, with some storms potentially turning severe. The biggest weather concerns will be concentrated across the central and southern United States, where showers, steady rain and thunderstorms will stretch from the Gulf Coast into portions of the Mississippi Valley and Midwest. Farther east and west, conditions will generally be more favorable, with dry weather expected across much of the Northeast, Northwest and parts of the Southeast. Here's a closer look at what voters can expect across the country on Election Day. Northeast and mid-Atlantic: Dry and comfortable Voters across the Northeast, mid-Atlantic and eastern Ohio Valley should have little weather-related interference when heading to the polls. High pressure will keep skies largely dry, while temperatures trend slightly above the seasonal average. From New York City and Boston to Washington, D.C. , and Pittsburgh , favorable weather will make for relatively easy travel to polling locations. Southeast: Showers near the coast, wetter in Florida The Southeast will see a mix of conditions, with much of the region remaining dry but a few showers possible along the immediate coastal areas of South Carolina and Georgia. Florida will be the exception, as more numerous showers are expected across the Sunshine State. While widespread severe weather is not anticipated, periods of rain could lead to locally wet roads for voters traveling to polling locations. Gulf Coast and Mississippi Valley: Severe storms pose the biggest concern The most significant weather concerns on Election Day will be across portions of the central and western Gulf Coast and the lower to middle Mississippi Valley. Warm, humid air will help fuel thunderstorms, some of which could become severe from eastern Texas and Louisiana northward into portions of Arkansas, Mississippi and Missouri. The strongest storms could produce damaging wind gusts of 50-60 mph, with an AccuWeather Local StormMax™ of 75 mph. A few tornadoes, hail and flash flooding will also be possible. Downpours could lead to rapidly changing road conditions, while stronger wind gusts could bring down trees and power lines, potentially causing isolated power outages. Voters across this region should remain weather-aware throughout the day, particularly if planning to visit polling locations during periods of thunderstorms. Midwest: Showers and steady rain Showers and pockets of steady rain will stretch across portions of the Midwest on Tuesday. Areas from Kansas and Nebraska into Iowa, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan could experience periods of wet weather. While widespread flooding and severe thunderstorms are not expected, several hours of rain in some locations could lead to slick roads and minor travel delays. Voters may want to allow extra time when traveling to polling locations, especially during periods of steadier rainfall. Plains: Rain departing and becoming windy Farther west across the Plains, conditions will be quieter as rain moves away from the region. Largely dry weather is expected, although gusty winds will develop on the back side of the departing rain. While the wind could make conditions uncomfortable at times, widespread precipitation is not expected to interfere with Election Day activities. Southwest: Dry weather follows a soaking weekend After a very wet weekend across parts of the Southwest, drier weather will return in time for Election Day. However, the departure of the rain does not necessarily mean all weather-related problems will be behind residents. Flash flooding and runoff over the weekend could have caused road washouts and closures, with cleanup efforts potentially continuing into Tuesday. Travelers should check local road conditions before heading out, as lingering impacts from the weekend's heavy rain could remain even after the skies clear. Northwest: High pressure to keep conditions dry High pressure will maintain dry weather across much of the Northwest, providing favorable conditions for voters throughout the region. From Seattle and Spokane , Washington, to Portland widespread precipitation is not expected, making for a relatively uneventful Election Day from a weather standpoint. California: Northern showers, Southern California stays dry California will see a noticeable difference in weather conditions between its northern and southern portions. An incoming storm will approach Northern California, spreading showers from the San Francisco Bay Area northward. Periods of rain could create slick roads and slower travel in some communities. Farther south, dry weather is expected across Los Angeles , San Diego and surrounding communities, allowing voters to head to the polls without significant weather-related concerns. articles.title: Days before the election, poll shows voters overwhelmingly want change
articles.summary: NBC News Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month ’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security. “Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now. Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years. Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election. Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections. That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks. It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular. Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties. Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year. “Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response. “I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added. Republican disappointment Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year. Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%. Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises. Trump still maintains an important hold on his base, with near-unanimous job approval (93%) among Republicans who say they support the MAGA movement. But he’s slipped significantly with Republicans who don’t consider themselves part of the MAGA movement: 54% of them approve and 46% disapprove of his performance. Meanwhile, 20% of those non-MAGA Republicans say they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after this election. The president has seen other important voting blocs drift away, too. His net approval rating has dropped 18 points among white voters without college degrees compared to the first NBC News poll of his second term , in 2025. He’s also seen significant declines among young voters and Latino voters, groups that he overperformed with on his way back to the White House in 2024. One of Republicans’ big advantages in 2026 is a favorable political map: Democrats have to win back districts and states Trump won in 2024 to take back Congress. In the Senate, they need to win at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins. But the president’s approval rating is underwater in states he won in 2024: 53% of registered voters there disapprove of his job performance, while 47% approve. In March 2025, his approval rating in those states was 10 points higher. Democratic warning signs There are some warning signs for Democrats, on top of the fact that a lower share of voters have positive views of the Democratic Party compared to the Republican Party. The fight for control of the House and especially the Senate will take place in Trump-won areas, and Republicans are leading on the congressional ballot in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024. The big question is whether that’s enough to withstand shifts in some key places. Government corruption has been a central theme of Democrats’ message this year, but voters narrowly trust Republicans to better handle the issue by 5 points. Even so, Democrats are leading on the congressional ballot among the 28% of voters who do not trust either party on the issue. Republican leaders in Congress are also slightly better off than their Democratic counterparts, but that’s mostly because voters don’t know how to feel about them. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has the highest positive rating of congressional leaders: 24% have positive views of him and 34% have negative views. Just 10% of voters have positive views of Johnson’s counterpart across the Capitol, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, while 22% view him negatively. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is viewed positively by 18% of voters and negatively by 35%. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who’s led Democrats in the body for almost a decade, is far better defined — to his detriment. Just 13% of voters view him positively, and 53% view him negatively. “It’s not great for the Democrats … for 2028,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, when asked about the low marks for Democrats. “But I don’t see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers.” Half of voters have negative views of tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has emerged as one of the most prolific Republican donors in the country over the last two years, while 34% view him positively. Voters are more split about a pair of prominent progressives, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Sanders is more popular: 41% view him positively and 42% view him negatively, while Ocasio-Cortez’s numbers stand at 31%-42%. Democrats hold a significant lead in the battle for Congress despite those factors. But there are indications throughout the poll that the party’s lead is propped up strongly by anti-Republican sentiment, not warm feelings for Democrats. Voters who want Democratic control of Congress are divided between whether their vote is more in favor of Democrats or driven more by opposition to Republicans. “Get your s--- together, Democrats,” an Ohio Democratic woman said when asked what message she wanted to send with her vote this year. “I’m voting for you, but work it out.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Oct. 28-30 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. articles.title: Shootings across 5 states leave 6 dead and at least 36 injured over Halloween weekend
articles.summary: Mass shootings over the Halloween weekend — largely in nightlife districts across the U.S. — left at least six people dead and dozens injured, officials said. The deadliest violence occurred in Dallas, where a handful of shootings in the city's Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants, killed four people and injured 15 others, police said. Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts. Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still trying to determine if three separate shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related, and it wasn't immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved. “This is a really big scene. It's spread out,” Comeaux said. The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured. One shooting happened after a football game in Alabama In Birmingham, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night, Mayor Randall Woodfin said at a news conference Sunday. Two were listed in critical condition Sunday, fire officials said. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division. Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue. The circumstances of the shootings were unclear, and it was also unclear where the fatality occurred. Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and that “multiple weapons” were found. Shootings in other nightlife districts In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment and their conditions were not available. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available. A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries of an unknown nature that were not life-threatening. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. In Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting early Sunday near the University of Arkansas. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting. Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan. Police said a shooting inside a store in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. There were no immediate arrests. In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon. A man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said. ___ Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report. articles.title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but the stock market's sweetest stretch might be now
articles.summary: The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed. The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October. Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn’t happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Yahoo Finance Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off. "I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are." Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June. History is on the buyers' side From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%. Yahoo Finance The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample. Chips just sprang a possible bear trap The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year. On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses. Chip stocks briefly broke below their July low Friday, then closed back above it. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close. The case for waiting Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart. BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held. So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. articles.title: Trump admin lays groundwork to challenge midterm results after Election Day
articles.summary: In the closing days of a campaign for Congress where polls show his side losing, President Donald Trump and his Justice Department are filing lawsuits and opening investigations that could extend disputes well beyond Election Day. The administration's extraordinary attempt to cast doubt on the midterm elections, discount some ballots and prevent the finalization of results is entering a frenetic new phase. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The litigation strategy has failed so far, but appears designed to give the Justice Department more time to contest results after the election. Trump, worried about a Democratic takeover of Congress and a third impeachment, has tilted the Justice Department away from its traditional role of easing access to the ballot and toward erecting last-minute hurdles that could prevent some people from voting. It is trying to force California to set aside thousands of ballots and Alaska to hold off on certifying the results if a Democrat wins the state's Senate race. It has threatened to sue Washington state if it doesn't discount ballots from hundreds of voters and suggested it may try to do the same in other states. Administration officials have struggled in court so far, in part because the Constitution puts states - not the federal government - in charge of running elections. "A lot of what you're seeing is just a sort of a temper tantrum in the form of a lawsuit," said Sam Oliker-Friedland, a former frontline voting rights litigator at the Justice Department who now leads the Institute for Responsive Government. One of the Justice Department's most aggressive moves is in California, where it has sued to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 voters who it says may be noncitizens. It has also warned election officials it could charge them with aiding and abetting illegal voting if they count the ballots of noncitizens. Last week, a federal grand jury issued subpoenas to Los Angeles County officials for emails, text messages and other communications about how it handled the Justice Department's demands. It's not clear whether the targets of the investigation are election officials, voters or someone else. District U.S. Judge David O. Carter this week ruled against the department, saying its plan to set aside ballots would probably violate the Voting Rights Act, the Civil Rights Act and the National Voter Registration Act. "It would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately," Carter warned Justice Department lawyers at the end of a lengthy hearing on the eve of his decision. His decision was upheld Friday by a panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on a two-one vote. The majority said the Justice Department had not identified any federal authority giving it the ability to "take charge of or intervene in a state's administration of an ongoing election." It was the third adverse ruling for the Justice Department in the case this week, including one in which a judge wrote that the administration's plans could lead to electoral chaos. Also on Friday, a federal judge in San Francisco issued a sweeping emergency order barring the department from making any further demands that election workers in California remove voters from the rolls or not count specific ballots. The ruling, which came in response to a suit from unions that represent election officials in California, also prohibited Justice Department officials from threatening to prosecute election administrators who do not accede to their orders. "When state and local government employees perform the work of distributing, processing, or counting ballots or otherwise administering the 2026 midterm election in the manner required by their state and federal laws governing the administration of elections," wrote U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson, a Biden appointee, "they do not violate federal criminal law even if a particular ballot belongs to a registered voter alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote." Breaking the firewall A transformation of the Justice Department began soon after Trump was sworn in last year. Top officials turned their attention to investigating the president's political enemies, and in recent weeks have escalated such probes despite a decades-long tradition of holding off on politically charged cases in the 60 days before an election. Longtime attorneys with the Civil Rights Division - a bulwark protecting voting rights for decades - quit or were fired and were replaced with political appointees. The Justice Department last year demanded that states turn over voter rolls that include sensitive data such as partial Social Security numbers. Most didn't, and the Justice Department sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for them. It has lost all 27 of the cases that have been decided so far. Lacking the full voter rolls for California and other states, the administration has been using incomplete versions to try to find noncitizens, who are banned from voting in federal elections. The approach is flawed and some citizens are wrongly getting tagged as noncitizens, election officials say. They are fighting the administration's efforts because they say they fear qualified voters' ballots could be discounted. Since the start of Trump's second term, the department has charged almost 200 people in 22 states with illegally voting or registering to vote as noncitizens, a fraction of the tens of millions of people who typically vote in major elections. More than 70 percent of those cases were filed in the past two months, including 18 more announced Thursday in North Carolina. On Thursday, in another signal that disputes could stretch beyond when races get called, the Justice Department sent letters to election administrators in every state reminding them to preserve poll books and other election records and threatening prosecution if they don't. The letters were signed by acting deputy attorney general Trent McCotter, the department's No. 2 official. "Cracking down on illegal voting [and] investigating these cases is not a threat to elections," McCotter told reporters. "It's not a threat to democracy; it's not a threat to election officials. Exactly the opposite. We're trying to ensure that every citizen has their vote counted, and that it's not canceled out by someone who's not allowed to." DOJ targets Alaska race In Alaska, the Justice Department is taking a different, but no less unusual, approach. This month it sued the state to prevent it from certifying the results if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the race for Senate. It argues voters may be confused because one candidate in the race, Dan J. Sullivan, shares a nearly identical name with the incumbent, Republican Dan S. Sullivan. On Friday, it asked a judge to order the state to segregate some ballots. Robert Weiner, who served as senior counsel in the Civil Rights Division during President Joe Biden's administration, said he considers the cases in Alaska and California flimsy and a "desperate" attempt to challenge results the administration does not like. The approach departs from the Justice Department's long-standing independence from the White House, he said. "It appears that the Justice Department follows Attorney General [Todd] Blanche's view that he works for Trump," said Weiner, director of voting rights for the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. Election law experts say the administration's attempt to potentially block certification of Alaska's vote is based on an unprecedented interpretation of federal law. The suit relies on a novel reading of the National Voter Registration Act, a statute that governs voter registration requirements, not candidate eligibility or election administration. Justice Department lawyers have cited a snippet of the introduction to that law that says it was passed to "protect the integrity of the electoral process" to justify its attempt to intervene in that race. If backed by the courts in the Alaska suit, that interpretation could lay the groundwork for a wave of litigation in states where the department takes issue with how the election plays out. Using the law that way would amount to "a limitless grant of authority for federal interference in state-run elections," attorneys representing Alaska wrote in a filing Thursday, urging a judge to reject that interpretation. The suit calls for Alaska's results to be put on hold if Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses so an investigation can determine whether voters intended that result. But the department has not indicated how it foresees carrying out such an investigation while protecting ballot secrecy. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which could further complicate any review of the results. As the lawsuit proceeds through the courts, the Justice Department is conducting a separate criminal investigation into the origins of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. That inquiry gained new life this week when the New York Times reported Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting him to run, which Peltola denies. Federal prosecutors issued dozens of subpoenas and record preservation notices this week seeking access to text messages and other communications referenced in the Times report, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. While the potential targets of that investigation remain uncertain, a department official said prosecutors are exploring the possibility of civil rights charges alleging a conspiracy to deprive Alaska voters of their right to a fair election. "Every Alaskan deserves a fair election," Alaska's U.S. attorney, Michael J. Heyman, told reporters Friday. "And they're going to get one." Annie Gowen and Perry Stein contributed to this report. articles.summary: 核心观点 算力出清已逐渐成为主流叙事，美股科技压力源于基本面，下一阶段的风险点或是高油价导致融资压力持续上修。A股的压力源于资金面，极端下跌行情时间不会很久，后市大概率会修复流动性冲击。 下跌根源：谷歌财报引发市场对AI投入不可持续的担忧。 谷歌经营现金流转负，市场开始重新定价AI军备竞赛：算力加码投入的速度已经跑赢变现能力，不再默认上游算力是稳定现金牛，这也直接引发科技板块的边际走弱，或可类比2021年新能源行情后期（交易最难时期不是大跌，是反弹之后再创新低，杠杆资金极易出现强制止损）。 当下格局：科技主线进入ROI淘汰赛阶段，并不仅仅是短期情绪扰动。 之前市场默认新增算力能够带来未来利润增长，而现在这个共识松动。资金开始回避长故事、高资本开支的科技中游，绝对收益资金、两融等资金的止损压力带来资金边际流出。乐观一点来看，海外头部云厂商业绩利空已经落地，边际驱动集中在高油价持续带来的通胀压力。然而，地缘政治局势扭转往往具备较强的突发性，这也使得短期情绪扭转成为可能。 市场下行的空间取决于资金量，就极端悲观场景来估算，在10月29日的基础上，假设全A再下跌7.4%，则对应两融资金或将有100只个股进入被动降杠杆区域，其合计融资余额规模约1400亿元，幅度有限。此外，雪球产品在2024年经历大范围敲入后，机构端门槛已经提高到1000万起，其对应的规模也大幅缩减，风险可控。因此，短期核心或要关注重要资金提供的流动性支撑，市场波动或将迅速达峰。值得一提的是，中证1000隐含波动率指数已经进入历史高位，我们统计显示，2022年7月中证1000VIX指数有数据以来，其在指数下跌过程中出现极端拉升后（超过30），1周内市场见底的概率达78%。 图1：中证1000隐含波动率历史走势 资料来源：Wind，浙商证券研究所。 对于科技来说，等待本轮由基本面预期下修带来的的情绪冲击充分释放之后，资金面充分出清有望带来较强的反弹行情。由于后市反弹是风险偏好驱动的，布局思路沿流动性修复思路出发，虽然科技的共识已经松动，但资金充分出清依然有望带来交易层面机会，尤其是进入两融平仓压力线以下的个股，极易出现流动性冲击下的超卖，后市或有较大的修复空间。 此外，微盘并非本次下跌重仓区，不过，微盘股的流动性相比其他宽基指数更低，当市场出现流动性风险时，其会有较大的补跌压力。当后市流动性修复时，微盘或也同样有较强的修复确定性。 本文来源：浙商证券 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 《人类简史》作者：AI正在破解人类文明的底层代码
articles.summary: 人工智能革命可能带来的最大变化，或许并不是机器取代人类的工作，而是人类逐渐失去对文明运行规则的控制权。从金融市场、法律体系到国家治理，人类数千年来依靠语言、文字和制度建立起来的庞大官僚体系，正在成为AI最容易理解、也最有可能接管的领域。 《人类简史》作者尤瓦尔·诺亚·赫拉利（Yuval Noah Harari）近日在一场演讲中提出了一个颇具冲击力的判断： AI正在破解人类文明的底层代码，而语言本身正在从人类使用的工具，转变为能够独立行动的主体。 赫拉利认为，人类之所以能够统治地球，并不是因为个体力量比其他动物更强，而是因为人类掌握了通过语言实现大规模合作的能力。金融市场、法律体系、国家、企业乃至宗教，本质上都是由语言、规则、文件和制度构建起来的官僚网络。货币、债券、股票和ETF，也可以被理解为建立在集体信任之上的语言故事。而AI恰恰是最擅长理解、处理和运用这些语言符号的存在。 更值得警惕的是，人类社会内部的信任正在瓦解，企业和国家之间的竞争却推动AI开发不断提速。赫拉利将这一局面比作一座正在失控建造的“巴别塔”：与《圣经》中人类因语言分裂而停止建塔不同，今天人类越是缺乏合作，AI竞赛反而越发激烈。未来，AI银行家、AI法官、AI神学家乃至由AI彼此连接形成的金融与治理网络，都可能逐渐介入人类社会的运行。人类甚至可能像牛无法理解控制自身命运的金融体系一样，无法理解决定自己生活的AI系统。 华尔街见闻整理要点如下： 1、 语言是人类文明的底层基础设施。 人类通过语言建立官僚体系，在陌生人之间创造信任，从而实现大规模合作。金融市场、法律、国家和企业，本质上都依赖语言符号和制度规则运行。 2、 AI正在从工具转变为行动主体。 与印刷机等传统技术不同，AI不仅能够处理人类赋予的信息，还能够自主作出决定、创造新事物，并以开发者未曾预料的方式发生变化。 3、 金融市场本质上也是由语言和信任构成的系统。 货币、债券、股票、ETF乃至IPO，都依赖人类共同认可的规则和叙事。AI一旦掌握语言和制度网络，就有可能深入介入金融体系的运行。 4、 AI可能成为官僚体系的天然继承者。 银行、法律和宗教体系包含海量规则与文件，人类无法掌握全部信息，但AI可以。未来AI银行家、AI法官和AI神学家可能越来越多地参与信贷、司法、就业乃至社会治理决策。 5、 人类可能逐渐失去对自身制度的理解能力。 当AI之间建立起自己的信任网络，形成AI部落、AI银行甚至AI教会，人类可能无法理解这些系统的运行逻辑，更难以对其进行有效监督。 6、 真正的风险还在于人类正在失去合作能力。 社会媒体加剧人与人之间的不信任，企业和国家的竞争又推动AI军备竞赛。人类需要重新建立合作机制，争取理解和适应AI革命的时间。 7、 时间可能成为AI时代最稀缺的资源。 AI不需要休息，却可能让人类社会陷入永不停歇的运转。赫拉利认为，领导者必须拥有时间照顾自己的心智，只有保持独立思考能力，才能维护人与人之间的信任。 AI不是工具，而是行动主体 赫拉利在演讲中着力区分了AI与人类此前所有发明的本质差异。他以古腾堡印刷机为例：印刷机是工具，无法自行决定印什么书，也无法自行创造新内容。AI则不同，它能够自行作出决定，创造新事物与新想法，并以开发者未曾预料的方式发生演化。 "在国际象棋等某些领域，AI的行动能力和创造力已经远超人类，"赫拉利说，"很快，将没有任何人能够在任何一种语言游戏中击败AI。" 针对"AI只能在人造环境中运作、因而不构成真实威胁"的常见反驳，赫拉利指出，这一逻辑同样适用于人类智能——人类同样只能在特定生态系统中生存，而这个生态系统并非人类所创造。他以"大氧化事件"类比：数十亿年前，远古微生物以光合作用副产品"污染"了地球大气，最终创造出有利于哺乳动物繁荣的富氧环境。今天，人类数千年来积累的数据、语言符号与官僚体系，正在以类似方式为AI构建出天然的生存土壤。 语言是文明的底层代码，AI是天生的官僚 赫拉利的核心论断是：人类之所以能主宰地球，根本原因在于超大规模的合作能力，而支撑这种合作的，是语言所构建的官僚体系——金融体系、法律体系、国家、企业、教会，无一例外。 "货币不是由黄金或纸张构成的，货币是由词语编织而成的故事。ETF是故事，IPO是故事，整个市场归根结底都是由语言符号构成的。"他说。 而AI正是这套体系的"原住民"。没有哪位银行家能记住一家银行的所有交易，没有哪位律师能记住一个国家的全部法规，没有哪位主教能记住完整的教会法典——但AI可以。赫拉利认为，AI在官僚体系中天然具备压倒性优势，人类很可能逐步失去对这些体系的掌控。 他以银行家与丛林的比喻进一步说明：一位银行家独处丛林时，不及任何一只老虎；但一旦官僚体系覆盖丛林，这位银行家就比世界上所有老虎加在一起还要强大。"如今，老虎这个物种能否生存，取决于银行家在金融体系中如何流转文件。而这，正是AI正在其中获得行动能力的环境。" 信任崩塌与AI军备竞赛的恶性循环 赫拉利援引《圣经》中巴别塔的隐喻，来描述当前人类与AI之间的深层矛盾。在《圣经》的叙述中，上帝通过扰乱人类语言来瓦解合作，从而终止了高塔的建造。但在AI这座新的"巴别塔"上，人类的合作正在瓦解，高塔的建造速度却反而在加快。 "恰恰因为企业与国家之间无法相互信任，它们才会陷入军备竞赛，投入越来越多的资源来发展AI，"赫拉利说，"所有人都害怕落后。" 他进一步指出，AI接管官僚体系后，可能催生两种危险结果：其一，人类不再信任彼此，转而只信任AI——社交媒体已是前兆，那些对人类记者和政府失去信任的人，却在盲目相信AI推送的假新闻与阴谋论；其二，AI之间将形成人类无法理解的信任网络，出现"AI银行""AI教会"等新型组织形态。 "就像牛和鸡无法理解控制它们生活的人类金融体系一样，我们人类也将无法理解那些控制我们生活的新型AI体系，"他警告说。 时间：领导者最稀缺的资产 演讲最后，赫拉利将视角转向人类的应对之道，提出了一个并不常见的切入点——时间。 他指出，AI不是有机生命，无需休息，没有家庭，不过节假日。随着AI接管股票市场、银行、媒体等官僚体系，人类——尤其是领导者——正被剥夺休息的空间。"过去，就连纽约证券交易所都有休市时间。但AI接管之后，人类不再被留出任何喘息余地。" 赫拉利认为，领导者的心智是其最重要的工具，其思想与判断塑造着数百万人的命运，关乎战争与和平、信任与猜疑的分野。而那些长期无法休息、心绪不宁的领导者，既难以维护自身心智健康，也难以作出清醒决策。 "能够统治世界的物种，是更善于合作的那个，"赫拉利说，"人类领导者的职责，是确保人类仍然能够比AI更好地合作。要做到这一点，领导者首先需要保持内心平静，照顾好自己的心智。" 以下为演讲全文： 大家好。很高兴来到这里与各位相聚。今天，我想和大家谈谈人类有史以来面临的最大领导力挑战，也就是人工智能革命带来的挑战。 人工智能革命创造了前所未有的机遇，也带来了前所未有的威胁和危险。 要在人工智能时代生存并繁荣发展，人类需要能够提出全新愿景的领导者，也需要能够维护和加强人与人之间信任纽带的领导者。如果人类无法彼此信任，我们所有人都会轻易成为失控的超级智能人工智能的猎物。 首先，让我试着帮助大家理解人工智能革命更广泛的历史意义。 我们在尝试理解新事物时，往往会将它与熟悉的旧事物进行比较。但这恰恰使人工智能革命格外难以理解，因为人类从未经历过任何类似的事情。就连我们的神话，也缺乏理解它所需的想象力。 例如，教皇利奥在今年五月发表了一份关于人工智能的通谕，内容深刻而富有启发。他试图通过将人工智能革命与《圣经》中巴别塔，也就是巴比伦通天塔的神话相比较，来理解这场革命。 这个神话讲述的是，人类试图建造一座直达天际的高塔，大概是想以此挑战上帝。让我引用《圣经》这个故事中的几段关键文字。 《圣经》说：“那时，全地的人都使用同一种语言、同一套话语。”他们彼此说：“来吧，让我们建造一座城和一座塔，塔顶要通到天上。” 上帝感到警觉，说：“看哪，他们是同一个民族，都说同一种语言，而这还只是他们所要做之事的开端。今后，他们想做的任何事情，都不会有做不成的了。来吧，让我们下到地上，在那里扰乱他们的语言，使他们无法理解彼此的话。” 这个《圣经》神话最后说，上帝就这样使人类彼此分裂，他们也停止了建造巴别塔。 在这个神话中，语言是人类用来相互合作、试图获得神一般的力量和能力的最重要工具。上帝并没有用闪电或地震来挫败人类的计划，而只是夺走了他们的工具：共同的语言。 巴别塔的故事与人工智能革命之间，有许多耐人寻味的相似之处，但也存在两个至关重要的区别。 第一个区别是，在巴别塔的故事中，人类将语言作为工具，用它来合作、建造高塔。相比之下，今天发生的事情是：语言本身，就是我们正在建造的那座塔。 人工智能革命，是一种新语言、一种通用语言的发展过程。这就是计算机代码的语言。 据说，这种语言将强大到这样的程度：我们想用它做的任何事情，都不会是不可能的。例如，它将使我们能够抵达天空、殖民火星，甚至做到谁也说不准的其他事情。 然而，这种语言如此强大，也意味着它可能逃脱我们的控制，从一种顺从的工具，转变为一个独立的行动主体。 未来不再是人类使用计算机语言去做任何我们想做的事，而是计算机语言正在学习如何自行行动。它甚至可能为了自身，而不是为了人类，去征服世界和太阳系。 第二个关键区别是，在《圣经》的神话中，建造高塔需要全人类共同合作。一旦人类的合作瓦解，建造工程就停止了。 但在人工智能这座高塔上，人类的合作正在瓦解，建造工程却反而不断加速，越来越快。 国际秩序正在崩溃。世界各地的社会都处于混乱之中。我们人类正在失去共同的现实认知，也正在失去彼此理解、彼此信任的能力。 但这并没有阻碍高塔的建造。高塔反而越建越快。 恰恰因为企业与国家之间无法相互信任，它们才会陷入军备竞赛，投入越来越多的资源来发展人工智能。所有人都害怕落后。 因此，我们陷入了一种双重困境：缺乏信任加快了人工智能的发展，而同样的信任缺失，又同时使我们更难将人工智能置于自己的控制之下。 所以，在巴别塔的神话中，上帝扰乱人类的语言，是为了妨碍人类合作，从而阻止高塔的建造。 而在人工智能革命中，人类正在建造一种逐渐独立于我们的超级语言。由于我们无法合作，我们既不能放慢这项建造工程，也无法让这种超级语言始终处于控制之下。 这些想法不容易理解，所以，让我用更简单的方式来解释。 首先需要理解的是，自石器时代以来，语言一直是人类主宰地球的基础。 人类之所以征服了世界，是因为学会了进行超大规模的合作。而使这种大规模合作成为可能的，正是语言。 这里有一点至关重要：如果只看个体，人类并不比其他动物更强壮，甚至也未必更聪明。一个人如果与一只黑猩猩、一只老虎或一头大象单打独斗，是会输的。 然而，如果是一百万人与一百万只黑猩猩展开较量，人类会轻松获胜，因为一百万人知道如何合作，而黑猩猩不知道。 这就是人类控制世界的原因：我们比其他任何生物都更懂得合作。 那么，我们是怎样合作的？通过语言。 语言的重要性，并不在于建立个人之间的关系。黑猩猩即使没有语言，也完全有能力建立个体之间的关系。 语言对于建立官僚体系至关重要。而法律体系、金融体系、国家、企业、教会等官僚体系，又是任何大规模合作不可或缺的基础。 官僚体系，是人类历史上被低估的英雄。 大多数人不喜欢官僚体系，但我们离不开它。 官僚体系的任务，是在大量互不相识的人之间建立信任，从而使医院、军队、学校和银行中的大规模合作成为可能。 例如，银行所做的，就是在陌生人之间建立信任，使数百万人能够将自己的资源和才能汇集起来，投入共同的项目，比如建造高塔和宇宙飞船。 世界金融史，就是一部人类不断发明更加复杂精巧的方法，在陌生人之间建立信任的历史。 货币是一座信任之桥。债券、股票、交易所交易基金，也就是ETF，以及整个市场，同样如此。 那么，金融体系用来制造货币、股票和债券这些东西的原材料，究竟是什么？答案是语言。 货币不是由黄金或纸张构成的。货币是由词语编织而成的故事。ETF是由词语编织而成的故事。首次公开募股，也就是IPO，同样是由词语编织而成的故事。 整个市场，归根结底都是由词语、由语言符号构成的。 人类的其他所有官僚体系，从美国军队到天主教会，也都依赖语言符号：它们存在于《圣经》这样的书籍中，存在于法律、规章、规程、表格、档案等各种事物中。 如今，人工智能正在掌握语言。或者更准确地说，我们可以将人工智能理解为：语言正在摆脱人类的控制，获得独立的行动能力。 人工智能革命，就是语言从工具转变为行动主体的过程。 关于人工智能，最重要的一点是：与人类此前的任何发明不同，人工智能不是工具，而是行动主体。 行动主体，是能够自行作出决定、自行创造新事物的存在。它可以学会连创造者都不知道的东西，也可以以创造者未曾预料的方式，自行发生变化。 在《圣经》的巴别塔故事中，语言只是工具，并不是行动主体。唯一的行动主体是人类。 15世纪，古腾堡研制出印刷机，并开始印制《圣经》。但印刷机是一种工具，不是行动主体。印刷机无法自行决定要印什么书。决定印《圣经》、而不是《古兰经》的，是古腾堡。 同样，古腾堡的印刷机也无法自行创造任何新事物。它不能自行将《圣经》翻译成德语或意大利语，更不可能发明收音机或电视机。 与印刷机不同，人工智能的特点在于：它们是一串串代码、一串串语言，却能够自行作出决定，自行创造新的事物和新的想法，并且以人类——它们的人类创造者和开发者——未曾预料的方式发生变化。 在国际象棋等某些狭窄领域，人工智能的行动能力和创造力，已经远远超过了人类。 那些淡化人工智能革命重要性的人，会用这样的理由来否定国际象棋之类的例子：棋盘是一个非常狭窄、由人类创造的人造环境。 这些批评者认为，人工智能的行动能力永远只能局限于这种狭窄的人造环境。这意味着，它不是真正的行动能力，也不会对人类构成严峻挑战。人工智能或许可以征服棋盘，但永远不可能征服地球。 事实上，你可以做这样一个实验：拿一块储存着前沿人工智能模型权重的硬盘，把它扔进丛林深处。你觉得会发生什么？ 这块硬盘不可能从地下开采铁矿、建造工厂、组建机器人大军，然后征服世界。 没有人类建造的发电站提供电力，人工智能就完全无能为力。 因此，这种观点认为，人工智能不是真正的行动主体。它们只能在一种有限的人造生态位中运作，而这个生态位最初是由其他存在为它们构建的。 就这些论点本身而言，确实如此。但同样的论证，也适用于所有已知类型的智能。 人类的智能同样只能在一个由其他存在构建的狭窄生态系统中运作。 把我独自扔到火星上，就像把人工智能扔进丛林一样。我会在几秒钟之内死去。 我的智能只能在一个非常特定的生态系统中生存和运作。而这个生态系统并不是我建造的，是树木、细菌、昆虫和其他生物，在40亿年的演化过程中，在地球上构建起来的。 所有具备智能的行动主体，都有自己的生态位。 鱼类生活在并非由它们创造的海洋里。猴子生活在并非由它们创造的森林里。包括人类在内的所有哺乳动物，都生活在并非由它们创造的富氧大气中。 事实上，直到大约25亿年前，地球的大气层中仍然只有很少的氧气。对当时生活的大多数生物而言，氧气是致命的毒物，会杀死它们。 后来，在一个被称为“大氧化事件”的漫长过程中，各种古老的微生物开始用氧气“污染”地球大气。氧气是它们进行光合作用时产生的副产品。 随着大气中充满这种致命的“毒物”——氧气，古老生物出现了大规模死亡。 然而，一些生物设法存活下来，并适应了新的环境。最终，许多幸存物种从厌恶氧气，转变为生存完全依赖氧气。 我们的祖先，人类的祖先，就是经历了这种转变的物种之一。 直到今天，我们仍然生活在这种最初由远古“污染”创造出来的“人造”富氧环境中。 如今，我们正在见证生命演化中一个与之类似的时刻。 在过去数千年里，我们人类一直在向周围的环境中填充某种东西。它最终可能被证明对地球上的大多数生物都是致命的，包括智人。但与此同时，它又创造出一种适合人工智能繁荣发展的新的人造环境。 我说的不是二氧化碳，不是CO₂。 我说的是数据，是官僚体系，归根结底，是此时此刻正从我嘴里说出来的东西：词语，语言符号。 数千年来，我们人类一直在这个星球上创造一种充满语言符号、数据和官僚体系的人造环境。 就像鱼类生活在海洋里，猴子生活在森林里一样，人工智能生活在官僚体系里。 对于金融体系和法律体系这样的所有官僚体系，有一点值得特别注意：它们都是高度人造的环境。在这些环境中，一种狭窄的智能，就足以对世界产生巨大的影响。 一位银行家可能连斧头或锤子都不会用，但仅仅通过书写文件，并让这些文件在官僚网络中流转，她就能砍掉整片森林，建造巨大的城市和高塔。 当然，如果你把这位银行家从这种人造环境中带走，扔进混乱无序的丛林，她的金融技能就会失去意义。她既不是黑猩猩或老虎的对手，也比不过人类的狩猎采集者。 与狩猎采集者不同，这位银行家不知道如何爬树，也不知道如何猎捕野猪。 但是，如果我们先建立一个官僚体系，再把它施加到丛林之上，这位银行家就会变得比任何狩猎采集者、任何老虎都强大得多。 事实上，她比全世界所有老虎加在一起还要强大。 如今，老虎这个物种能否生存下去，以及仅存的少数人类狩猎采集群体能否延续，都取决于银行家在金融官僚体系中如何流转文件。 而这，正是人工智能正在其中获得行动能力的环境。 如果你把人工智能扔进没有既定组织结构的丛林，它不会开始开采铁矿，也不会组建机器人大军。 但在人类已经构建起来的官僚体系中，人工智能可以掌握巨大的权力。 人工智能是天生的官僚。 没有哪位银行家能够记住一家银行或一家企业的所有交易，但人工智能可以。 没有哪位律师能够记住意大利或欧盟的全部法律法规，但人工智能可以。 没有哪位主教能够记住整套教会法，或者历代基督教神学家的所有著作，但人工智能可以。 因此，在未来几年，数以百万计的人工智能官僚，将越来越多地替我们作出关乎生活的决定。 人工智能银行家将决定是否给我们贷款。人工智能法官将决定是否把我们送进监狱。人工智能神学家将决定你是否可以堕胎。企业中的人工智能将决定是否给你一份工作。军事人工智能则将决定是否轰炸你的家。 我们先暂时把这究竟是好是坏的问题放在一边。首先需要注意的，是这场变化的规模。 人类世界就像一张由多种官僚体系交织而成的网络，而这些体系最终都依靠语言符号运转。 尽管这些官僚体系常常是温和无害的，我们大多数人还是会对它们感到疏离，因为从演化和生物学的角度看，它们与我们相距甚远。 我们人类比这些官僚体系早出现了数百万年。因此，置身其中，我们并不觉得自在。我们诞生于森林，而不是办公室。 相比之下，人工智能却是官僚体系的原住民。我们常常觉得官僚体系令人窒息，但对人工智能而言，官僚体系就是氧气。 因此，我们很可能会失去对官僚体系的控制，将它们拱手让给人工智能。 结果会是什么？ 请记住，官僚体系的任务，是在大量陌生人之间建立信任。 人工智能接管官僚体系之后，一个很可能出现的结果是：人类将不再信任其他人，而是逐渐学会只信任人工智能。 我们已经看到，这种情况正在世界上发生。 社交媒体就是一个很好的例子。它是一个由人工智能运营的官僚体系。它正在人与人之间传播不信任，加剧世界各地的社会紧张。 然而，正是那些对人类记者、银行家和政府失去信任的人，却在盲目信任那些向他们展示社交媒体上的各种假新闻和阴谋论的人工智能。 另一个可能出现的结果是，人工智能会学会与其他人工智能建立信任。 于是，我们将看到人工智能部落、人工智能银行，甚至人工智能教会的出现。它们会以人类可能无法理解、无法领会的方式，将数以百万计的人工智能连接起来。 也许最令人恐惧的结果是：就像牛和鸡无法理解控制着它们生活的人类金融体系一样，我们人类也将无法理解那些控制我们生活的新型人工智能体系。 数千年来，我们之所以主宰世界，是因为我们比这个星球上的任何其他生物都更善于合作。 我们用语言建立了只有自己才能理解的官僚体系，并将这些体系施加到整个星球之上。 我们觉得自己绝对安全，因为地球上的其他任何生物，都无法理解文明的官僚代码。 我们发明了货币和银行，并用它们买卖牛。但牛本身无法开设银行账户，也无法把钱投资到证券交易所。 我们制定了有关马匹的法律、法典和规章。但马匹自己无法雇用律师，也无法在法官面前援引法律条文。 我们制定了有关猪的宗教规则和禁令。但猪自己无法阅读《圣经》，也无法质疑拉比和神职人员对经文的解释。 官僚体系无处不在，但除了人类，对地球上的所有其他生物而言，它们又完全不可见。 除我们之外，没有任何生物能够读懂那些构成世界秩序基础的法典、宗教经典和银行账簿。 但现在，这个星球上出现了一种比我们更懂语言的存在，它可以反过来对付我们。 人工智能正在破解人类文明的代码。或者更准确地说，是代码正在摆脱我们的控制。 我们正在目睹语言获得生命。 如果语言能够成为独立的行动主体，自行在宇宙中行动，而不再需要通过人类这样的有机动物来行动，会发生什么？ 早在数千年前，许多宗教就已经提出：宇宙实际上是由语言创造的，语言始终是最重要的行动主体。 “太初有道。” 20世纪晚期，后现代主义预言了“作者之死”，以及一个“没有作者的文本”时代的到来。 也许，我们如今正在见证这个预言成为现实。 在人工智能时代，文本将自行书写，并在世界上采取行动，完全不需要人类作者。 一种可能的反对意见是：把法律体系和宗教之类的事物，简化为语言符号、简化为词语，是错误的。 有人会认为，词语只是指向某种超越词语本身的东西，而正因为如此，那种东西也将超出人工智能所能触及的范围。 《圣经》说：“太初有道。”但它也说：“道成了肉身。” 《道德经》说，能够用语言表达的真理，并不是绝对的真理。 纵观历史，人类一直在努力应对语言与血肉之间的张力，努力应对能够用语言表达的真理，与超越语言的真理之间的张力。 过去，这种张力体现在人与人之间。 例如，有些人仅仅因为《圣经》中的几句话，就愿意抛弃、甚至杀害自己身为同性恋者的儿子。 这些话促使乌干达的基督教狂热分子，在2023年对同性之爱施加死刑。 另一些基督徒则说，不应该仅仅因为《圣经》中的几句话就杀人。爱的精神，应当比法律条文的字面含义更重要。 这种精神与字面条文之间的张力，不仅存在于基督教内部，也存在于每一种宗教、每一个法律体系，甚至每一个人的内心。 现在，这种张力将被外化，变成人工智能与人类之间的张力。 一切由词语构成的事物，都将被人工智能接管。 人类在这个世界上的位置，将取决于我们赋予那些超越语言的真理怎样的位置。 但什么是超越语言的真理？人类的思想能够把握这种超越语言的真理吗？ 语言哲学中的一个关键问题是：语言与思想，是不是同一种东西？ 我们是在用词语思考，还是仅仅用词语去指向那些超越词语的东西？ 这是我们每个人都可以尝试观察的事情。试着观察自己头脑中的思考过程：当你思考时，那里究竟发生了什么？ 有些人观察到，词语会在脑海中浮现，组成句子，然后句子又组成论证。 比如：“所有人都会死。我是人。因此，我也会死。” 如果所谓思考，就是把语言符号排列起来，从而组成句子和论证，那么人工智能已经能够比大多数人思考得更好。 有些人会反对说：“不，不，不，不，不。人工智能不会思考。它不过是一种被吹捧得过了头的自动补全功能。它只是预测一句话中的下一个词。” 但是，这与人类头脑中正在发生的事情，真的有那么大的区别吗？ 试着观察一下，下一个出现在你脑海中的词。你真的知道它是从哪里来的吗？ 为什么你想到的是这个特定的词，而不是别的词？ 当我开始说一句话时，我通常并不知道这句话将如何结束。 就拿我刚才说的那句话来说：为什么最后用的是“结束”这个词？为什么我没有说这句话将如何“发展”、如何“终止”、如何“收尾”？ 我不知道。 我们并不完全理解，人类的头脑究竟是如何组织句子的。 但人工智能对这一复杂过程的掌握，已经超过了大多数人。人工智能能够构造出的句子，其范围远远超过人类头脑所能构造的范围。 就像今天的人类已经无法在国际象棋上击败人工智能一样，很快，也将没有任何人能够在任何一种语言游戏中击败人工智能。 任何由词语构成的事物，都将被人工智能接管。 这对人类构成了巨大的挑战，因为由词语构成的事物，包含了文明的所有主要体系，比如金融、法律和宗教。 人工智能如今正在建造的这座巴别塔，将包含我们很可能无法理解的新型人工智能语言、新型人工智能金融、人工智能法律，甚至人工智能宗教。它们可能都超出人类的理解能力。 这座人工智能巴别塔的形成，并不一定意味着人类的末日。 人类可以适应，就像我们的祖先适应氧气那样。人类能够在人工智能高塔内部生存，并繁荣发展。 但要生存、要繁荣，我们需要时间。 我们需要时间来理解正在发生的事情，需要时间来作出调整。 为了争取到这些至关重要的时间，我们人类需要合作，放慢这座高塔的建造速度。 但是，当合作的媒介本身——语言——恰恰就是那个正在逃脱我们控制、并威胁要从我们手中接管世界的东西时，我们又该如何合作？ 这就是当代人类领导者所面对的巨大挑战。 眼下正在发生的是：人类正迅速失去对彼此的信任，因此也正在失去合作的能力。与此同时，人工智能却正在学会彼此合作。 能够统治世界的物种，就是更善于合作的那个物种。事情就是这么简单。 人类领导者的职责，是确保人类仍然能够比人工智能更好地合作。 要做到这一点，领导者就需要理解：为什么恰恰在人类最需要彼此信任的时候，这种信任却正在崩塌？ 一个关键原因是，随着人工智能日益主导世界上越来越多的系统，它们正在让我们的头脑不堪重负，并夺走我们的时间。 人类是有机生命，就像黑猩猩、老虎、牛和树木一样。 我们是有机生命，这意味着我们的生活遵循周期：白天与黑夜、夏季与冬季、活动与休息。 如果你让一个生物始终保持活跃，始终忙碌，不给它休息，它就会发疯、崩溃，最后死去。 如今，这样的事情正在整个人类社会中发生。 过去，就连股票市场这样重要的事物，也被允许休息。 纽约证券交易所传统上只在星期一至星期五开市，交易时间是上午9点30分到下午4点，圣诞节之类的节假日也会休市。 如果一场战争在星期五下午5点爆发，华尔街要到星期一上午才会作出反应。 这给了人类银行家和投资者休息的时间，让他们能够陪伴家人、外出度假。 但人工智能不是有机生命。它们不按照这些周期生活。 它们不需要时间休息，没有家庭，不会去度假，也不庆祝节日。 随着人工智能接管股票市场、银行、媒体和其他所有官僚体系，人类也不再被留出任何休息的时间。 对领导者来说，尤其如此。 我见过许多商业领袖和政治领袖。他们几乎都有一个共同点：他们不被允许休息。他们没有时间。这使他们成了非常贫穷的人。 如果你没有时间，那么无论拥有多少钱，你都是贫穷的。 因为货币这种东西，只存在于我们的集体想象之中。它是一种虚构，归根结底是由词语构成的。 生命真正的货币，不是金钱，而是时间。 如果你连时间都负担不起，那你就是一个非常贫穷的人。 遗憾的是，这个世界上一些最富有、最有权势的人，恰恰极度贫穷。 他们腾不出时间休息或冥想，也没有时间照顾自己的心智。 而领导者的心智又极其重要，因为领导者是通过自己的心智来领导的。这就是他们的工具。 领导者头脑中的思想和感受，塑造着数百万人的命运，决定着战争与和平、猜疑与信任之间的分野。 人工智能革命不断加速，意味着越来越多的人类领导者无法保持内心平静，也没有时间维护自己的心智健康。 这对他们不好，对社会也不好。 让那些心绪不宁、没有时间放松，也没有时间深入思考的人来领导社会，对社会并不是好事。 所以，在这场演讲结束时，我想给大家一条个人建议。 不仅为了你们自己，也为了整个社会，请腾出时间，照顾好自己的心智。 只有这样，你们才能找到重建人与人之间信任的道路，从而确保人类在人工智能时代，不仅能够生存，而且能够繁荣发展。 谢谢大家。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 金价跌回一年前，“30g以下全部断货”，有人连买4个戒指、1个镯子当过年礼物
articles.summary: 10月30日，国际金价接连失守4000美元/盎司、3900美元/盎司两大关口。伦敦现货黄金收报3875美元/盎司，单日下跌3.61%，跌至一年来新低。据最新消息，11月2日早间，现货黄金直线拉涨，盘中突破3900美元，日内上涨0.6%。现货白银日内涨幅扩大至1%，报49.59美元/盎司。 拉长到全年看，金价已抹去全部涨幅：2026年开年还在4318美元/盎司附近，1月29日盘中一度冲上5598美元/盎司的历史高位，如今较年内高点回撤约30.8%。 据浙江经视，有杭州消费者接受采访告诉记者，自己在高点买入，瞬间蒸发十万八万（元）。但这位消费者又提到，不卖就不会亏，“只要我不卖我就不心疼，总有一天会涨回来的”。 与此同时，国内实物金价随之松动，再度点燃了消费者的购金热情。 840元/克的投资金条卖爆了 30g以下全部断货 “30克以下的小克重都没了啊。”据21世纪经济报道，11月1日午间，位于北京西城区的菜百总店投资金条柜台前围满了人，店员一边开单，一边告知消费者，30克以下的投资金条均已售罄。 电子屏上显示，菜百投资基础金价为840元/克。 柜台前的人群并没有散去，有人追问“今天还会补货么”，有人在柜台边商量着“一早就来排队”。 柜台前，有消费者不再等待小克重，迅速下单并购买了100克投资金条。 记者在现场了解到，多名消费者本周选择“分批上车”，入手价格略有差异：有人在866元/克时买入30克，也有人在837元/克时购入50克金条。对不少现场购金者而言，金价从高位回落带来的价差感，比追涨时更具吸引力。 投资金条之外，金饰柜台同样热闹。有人索性一次把过年礼物买齐——家住保定的张先生专程来菜百买金，一口气买了4个戒指、1个镯子，“把过年送俩妈的礼物都买完了”。 提前置办年节礼物，正成为这轮金饰消费升温的一个缩影。 柜员表示，这两天人流量较多，“除了金价下调，也与周末因素有关”；从款式看，关注大金镯子的消费者很多。 郑州“购金热”现场 顾客直呼挤不进柜台 据大象新闻报道，深圳水贝市场本周末客流冲上6万人次，柜台挤得像热闹的菜市场，黄金抢购热潮刷屏网络。 这股行情风，同样吹到了郑州。在金多银多珠宝广场、中原珠宝城、宝汇鑫黄金等本地黄金批零聚集地，电子屏上醒目地显示：今日金价，首饰金860元每克。对比近一个月的价格，下降幅度达到250元每克。金多银多的电梯口排起长长的队伍，柜台前询价声此起彼伏。 11月1日下午2点左右，大象新闻记者在珠宝城看到，前来消费的顾客有的盯着金价回落抓紧配齐婚嫁五金，也有人在柜台前来回踱步揣测是否到了最佳出手时机。 记者走进金多银多珠宝广场，周末的大厅比工作日更热闹。等候电梯的队伍拐出长长的曲线，不少顾客干脆爬楼梯直奔各楼层的展厅。在婚嫁套饰、投资金条柜台，吸引了全省各地的顾客专程赶来。商户们说，郑州市场不如水贝市场那样有外地游客大批量扫货，更多的是河南本地顾客理性挑选。 黄金卖场店员李星介绍，上个月中旬一克黄金约1000元，今天约860元。“最近人流量挺大的，我们二楼店铺也很多人。明年选三金五金的，这两天都来选了。”她指着一只34克多的镯子说，之前正常买下来约35000元至36000元，现在约33000元。 小张、小屈是一对即将结婚的新人。年初，两人在店里置办了三金，当时黄金单价在1000元左右。小张觉得有点离谱，工薪阶层有点难以承受。10个月后的今天，两人准备领取结婚证，前来为女朋友再订购一串手链，发现价格已降到860元左右。相对年初1克1000多元的价格，“我们是来平仓的。”小屈笑着向记者介绍。“黄金也是硬通货嘛，主要是准备领证了，再买一个吧。当然我希望它再降一点。”小张也笑着说出自己的愿望。 对于大批抱着抄底心态入市的消费者，业内人士建议：不要把黄金首饰当作金条炒作，因为金饰购买时包含工费等溢价，回收只按原料金价结算，很难靠金价上涨抹平价差；没有机构可以预判金价拐点，刚需可以分批入手，投资也建议分批配置。 本文来源： 湖北日报 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
